title: The second case: the "to/for" form
goal: Master the case that prepositions demand most often, and the one you'll say most without noticing: the form used after *með*, *frá*, *að*, *hjá*, and *úr*.
bekal: form þágufall for all three noun genders
talk about means of transport, company, origin, and someone's place with the right preposition

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kaffi með vinum
dialogs.intro: Anna introduces Búdí to her friend Sigga. They make plans to see a movie that evening.

notes: **Þágufall (the dative) is the case prepositions demand most.** The six most common prepositions — *með*, *frá*, *að*, *hjá*, *úr*, *af* — **always** take it, no exceptions. Learn those six words with one example each and you already have half of what this case is used for.
**The endings are calm and predictable**: karlkyn and hvorugkyn words almost always end in **-i** (*skóli → skóla**num***, *hús → hús**inu***), kvenkyn words in **-u** (*vinkona → vinkon**u***).

**Fara með strætó literally "go with bus".** Means of transport always take *með* + þágufall: *með flugvél* (by plane), *með bíl* (by car), *með lest* (by train — though Iceland has no railway at all).

**Hjá means "at someone's place", not "near".** *Ég bý hjá vinkonu minni* = I live **at my friend's**. For "near" there's *nálægt*, also with þágufall. Remember *hjá pabba* in Unit 4 — now you know why it looked like that.

**Possessives change form too**: *húsið mitt* → *frá hús**inu** mín**u***; *vinkona mín* → *hjá vinkon**u** min**ni***. That's what makes Icelandic sentences feel heavy at first — not one word changes, but the whole string.

**Hlemmur is a place name, and even it changes**: *frá Hlemm**i***. Icelandic place names aren't frozen; they change form like any other noun. *Til Reykjavík**ur***, *frá Akureyr**i***, *í Vesturb**æ***.

grammars.title: Þágufall — how the endings change
body: Put it side by side with þolfall from Unit 8 and the difference jumps out: þolfall shortens, þágufall adds.
after: The forms **with the article** are the ones you'll use most, and their endings are distinctive: **-num** (kk), **-nni** (kvk), **-nu** (hk). These three sounds are the easiest þágufall markers to catch when listening.
Note that kvenkyn words often have **the same form** in þolfall and þágufall (*kirkju*, *bók*). That's good news: one form for two cases.

grammars.title: Pronouns in þágufall
body: You'll use these forms far more often than you'd expect, because almost every Icelandic expression of feeling uses them — that's Unit 14.
after: Note that *okkur* and *ykkur* are **the same** in þolfall and þágufall — two forms you don't need to choose between.
Only four are really new: *mér*, *þér*, *honum*, *henni*, plus *þeim*. Learn all five as one string; they show up in every unit after this.

blocks.title: Two pairs that are easy to mix up
items: **frá vs úr.** *Frá* is for origin in general (*frá Íslandi*), *úr* for coming **out of** something (*úr töskunni* — out of the bag). If you can replace "from" with "out of" without changing the meaning, use *úr*.

**að vs til.** Both mean "to", but *að* takes þágufall and means approaching (*að húsinu* — toward the house), while *til* takes eignarfall and means reaching a destination (*til Reykjavíkur*). The eignarfall case is covered in Unit 19.

blocks.text: Some verbs take þágufall directly, with no preposition in between. English only hints at this ("give **her** a book", "show **me**"), and Icelandic is not always logical about it — learn the case together with the verb.

*Gefa* takes two objects at once: the **receiver** in þágufall (*henni*) and the **thing given** in þolfall (*bók*). The order is exactly like English — "give her a book" — so you don't need to think about it.
